raw_response:
I am seventy years old, and these six mu have been in my hands for fifty years. I never went to school, but I know this soil by feel and smell. My household has six mouths, and some of my children work in the factories in Handan, so they send a little money home. That helps, but I still watch every fen. I have a well, so water is there when I need it, but pumping costs electricity, so I do not waste it.

This year I will split my six mu into three mu of cotton and three mu of spring maize. I have done this for a long time. It is my insurance — if cotton prices fall, I still have maize; if the maize gets hit by wind, I still have cotton. I thought about planting more cotton because the price was decent last year, but at my age I do not want too much back-bending picking. Three and three is balanced.

For the cotton, I will rotary till the soil in mid-April when the ground warms up. I will buy improved cotton seeds from the dealer — about three jin per mu, the kind called guoxinmian or similar. I trust these seeds; they have done well for me before. For fertilizer, I will spread one bag of compound fertilizer per mu as a base — the 15-15-15 kind that the shop keeps in stock. That is about fifty kilograms. When the plants flower, I will topdress with half a bag of urea. All together, that works out to about sixteen kilograms of nitrogen, eight kilograms of phosphorus, and eight kilograms of potassium per mu. I will irrigate twice: once right after planting if the spring is dry, and again in July when the bolls are forming. Cotton pests are relentless here — the bollworm always comes — so I will spray about fourteen times through the season, mostly insecticide and once for weeds. If the weather is normal, I expect about 550 kilograms of seed cotton per mu.

For the spring maize, I will rotary till in late April and plant hybrid seeds. Everyone uses hybrids now, even old farmers like me. One package per mu is enough. Maize needs more feed than cotton, so I will put down about eighty kilograms per mu of compound fertilizer — the 26-10-10 type. I will also topdress with a little urea at jointing. That comes to about twenty kilograms of nitrogen, eight kilograms of phosphorus, and eight kilograms of potassium per mu. I will irrigate three times: after sowing, when the stalk is knee-high, and when the ears are filling. For pests, three sprays will do — twice for insects and once for weeds. In a good year I get around 1,100 kilograms per mu.

My neighbor tried a fancy new cotton variety two years ago and had nothing but trouble. I will stick to what I know. The children told me to rest more, but as long as my legs hold up, I will farm. This plan has put food on our table for decades.
